idiom_name: forwarding class per interface (shared_ptr target, weak identity registry, atomic revoke flag)
implementation_notes: C++ has no reflection-based interception, so the membrane is a hand-written forwarding class per interface - or a policy-based template that generates one - holding a std::shared_ptr to the target, implementing the same interface and wrapping every argument it receives and every result it returns. Identity is the target pointer: the membrane registry maps it to the wrapper, holds the wrapper weakly (std::weak_ptr) so the registry does not extend target lifetimes or create cycles, and revocation is a shared flag (std::atomic<bool> or a generation counter) consulted before forwarding. The class-based form is the right choice whenever calls must actually be mediated; the operator-> template variant below only forwards, because once operator-> resolves to a plain pointer the built-in member access applies to the raw object and nothing can intercept the call.
pitfalls: operator-> cannot intercept the call it enables: once it yields a plain pointer the built-in member access runs on the raw object, so a generic template alias is a forwarding convenience, not a membrane - full mediation needs a forwarding class or ABI-level interposition.
A registry that owns the target keeps the whole graph alive and can form cycles (wrapper -> membrane -> registry -> wrapper); hold entries weakly and break the cycle deliberately.

Value semantics and slicing: a wrapper copied by value (or passed through a base-class parameter) can lose the membrane, so wrapped references must travel by pointer/reference and the wrapper must be non-sliceable (final, deleted copy) where that matters.

variants.name: Generic operator-> proxy template (forwarding alias)
variants.idiom_name: template wrapper whose operator-> forwards recursively to a plain pointer
variants.implementation_notes: The template form collapses the wrapper into one generic type: operator-> returns the target (or another object with operator-> of its own), and the language calls operator-> again on the result, recursively, until a plain pointer is reached and built-in member access applies. That makes it a transparent alias with a controlled lifetime - useful for ownership, logging at wrapper entry, or hiding a concrete type - but it mediates nothing: the call that follows executes on the raw object, so it cannot wrap results or arguments. Use it when the boundary needs indirection without a policy; use the forwarding-class variant when the boundary must enforce one.
pitfalls: Recursion ends at a raw pointer: whatever the last operator-> returns is called directly, so attenuation, wrapping of arguments and wrapping of results are all impossible through this route.

Dangling or expired targets: the alias holds a pointer or shared_ptr, and if the membrane revokes by clearing its registry the alias still holds a live target - revocation must invalidate the alias deliberately (clear the pointer, weak_ptr::lock, or a generation check).
